KEY MESSAGE 1...

A surface low pressure system and frontal boundary extending from 
the Great Lakes region down into the southern ADKs and central New 
England will continue to drift across the region through this 
evening. Hi-res models look to have the boundary reaching and 
stopping near I-90. The cold sector will be to the north of I-90 
with cloudy/overcast skies and highs in the upper 50s (terrain) and 
60s (valleys) while areas to the south of I-90 will be in the warm 
sector with slightly above normal tempertures in the upper 60s 
(terrain) and mid 70s (valleys) and will see more breaks of sun. 
Southerly winds will also be breezy through this evening. This 
system will help to continue periods of showers and some isolated 
thunderstorms for parts of the region this afternoon and evening. 
Current KENX radar, along with current CAMs guidance show a line of 
showers and isolated thunderstorms propagating out from the Great 
Lakes region across the southern ADKS and parts of the Mohawk Valley 
and Lake George and Saratoga Region, before shifting into parts of 
the southern Green Mountains and Berkshires later this evening.

While strong upper level winds will allow for 50+ kt of shear, 
surface based instability is limited with less than 500 J/kg 
available, the highest amounts of CAPE across more western areas of 
the ADKs and Mohawk Valley, and looks to be available only near or 
just after sunset. This timing of the ingredients and the lack of 
daytime heating from widespread cloud coverage in these areas should 
help to limit any storms that develop and weaken them as they 
approach our area. A Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5) for severe storms 
does extend into the western Mohawk Valley where the better chances 
for storms exists, but this appears to be a low threat for today. 
Even though there will be some bursts of heavier downpours within 
showers and thunderstorms, the threat for flooding concerns is also 
low. PWATs are near climatological normals across much of the region 
and slightly above the 75th percentile for areas I-90 north and west. 
Total expected rainfall is expected to be 0.75 to 1" with localized 
up to 1.5" in the far northern parts of Herkimer and Hamilton 
counties. Probabilistic guidance has a 75-95% chance for 1" or 
greater and a 30-40% chance for 2" or greater for areas north and 
west of I-90. Expected rainfall totals are much lower for the rest 
of the region with a 30% chance for 0.5" or greater for areas I-90 
south. 12z SPC HREF shows hourly rates should remain under 0.5" as 
well. While some ponding of water can't be ruled out on roadways and 
in poor drainage areas, total rainfall and rainfall rates appear 
beneficial for these areas. 

Another day of mild weather is expected again tomorrow before some 
cooler weather starts building towards the area for Wednesday night 
into Thursday. With high pressure overhead, Thursday looks to be a 
pleasant mostly sunny, but cool fall day with highs in the 50s and 
60s.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

The next frontal system and strong upper level trough arrives toward 
the end of the week bringing widespread rain showers across the 
region on Friday. Long range and ensemble models show that much of 
the rain will be steady through the day with the potential for a 
brief break sometime in the afternoon depending on the timing of the 
front, however confidence in the timing remains low. Rainfall totals 
at this time look to be manageable with NBM probabilistic guidance 
showing a 60-80% chance for 1" or greater in higher terrain areas 
north of the Capital Region and a 20-30% chance of 1" or greater in 
the Mid-Hudson Valley. The front looks to cross by Friday night from 
west to east with mainly dry conditions into the weekend outside of 
some light showers in higher elevations into Saturday morning. 

Temperatures turn chilly Friday night as the cold front passes 
through with most of the higher elevations below freezing and 
valleys dropping into the mid 30s Friday night. The upper level 
trough axis will be centered over the region by Saturday morning 
with 850 hpa temps dropping down to around -10 C, which is well 
below normal for mid October. As a result, daytime temps will only 
be in the 30s across the high terrain on Saturday, with 40s for 
valley areas. After a cold Saturday night, highs on Sunday will 
moderate somewhat, but will still be below normal (61 F).
In addition, a strong pressure gradient will result in breezy to 
gusty conditions, making it feel even colder through the weekend and 
making for a blustery late fall day. A strong upper level jet could 
mix down strong wind gusts on Saturday. Probabilistic guidance has a 
40% chance for gusts 40-45 mph which could be close to wind advisory 
range and knock down foliated trees and blow around any unsecured 
outdoors objects.
